items.question: Trace the evolution of poverty measurement in India from calorie-based lines to the multidimensional approach. How far does the National MPI represent an improvement over income-based estimates?
items.modelAnswer:
Poverty measurement in India has evolved from a **narrow calorie-anchored income line** to a **multidimensional view of deprivation**. The early approach, operationalised by the **Alagh Task Force (1979)**, fixed the poverty line at a minimum calorie intake — **2400 kcal/day (rural)** and **2100 kcal/day (urban)** — converted into consumption expenditure. The **Lakdawala Committee (1993)** refined this with **state-specific lines** and separate rural/urban price indices. The **Tendulkar Committee (2009)** marked a conceptual break: it **abandoned the pure calorie anchor**, adopted the **Mixed Reference Period (MRP)**, and folded in private spending on **health and education**, estimating poverty at **21.9% for 2011-12**. The **Rangarajan Committee (2014)** reverted to **separate rural/urban baskets** and a Modified MRP, yielding a higher **29.5%** — but the government did not officially adopt it, leaving a measurement vacuum.

The **multidimensional approach** addresses the core limitation of these income lines: poverty is more than low consumption. Using the **Alkire-Foster method**, the **Global MPI (OPHI-UNDP)** measures overlapping deprivations across **health, education and standard of living** (10 indicators). India's **National MPI (NITI Aayog)** adapts this to national priorities with **12 indicators**, adding **maternal health** and **bank accounts**, and draws on **NFHS** data. NITI's 2023 assessment showed the MPI headcount falling from **29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23)**, with about **24.82 crore** people escaping poverty.

The National MPI is an improvement in three ways: it captures **non-monetary deprivations** invisible to income lines; it is **actionable and scheme-linked** (each indicator maps to a flagship programme such as Ujjwala, Jal Jeevan or Jan Dhan); and it enables **district-level targeting**. Yet limits remain — it relies on periodic NFHS rounds, uses equal indicator weights, and does not capture income/consumption directly. The way forward is to treat income-poverty and MPI as **complementary**: the former for macro trends, the latter for targeting deprivations. For **Andhra Pradesh**, where welfare delivery is highly digitised, MPI-style indicator tracking dovetails naturally with the state's DBT and service-delivery platforms.
keyPoints: Alagh (1979) fixed calorie-based line (2400 rural/2100 urban kcal); Lakdawala (1993) added state-specific lines.
Tendulkar (2009) dropped calorie anchor, used MRP, included health/education spend — 21.9% (2011-12).
Rangarajan (2014) used separate baskets & Modified MRP — 29.5% (2011-12); not officially adopted.
MPI (Alkire-Foster) captures multidimensional deprivation; Global MPI = OPHI-UNDP, 3 dimensions/10 indicators.
National MPI (NITI) = 3 dimensions, 12 indicators (adds maternal health, bank accounts), NFHS-based.
NITI 2023: MPI headcount 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23); ~24.82 crore escaped poverty.
MPI is scheme-linked and enables district targeting but should complement, not replace, income-poverty estimates.
items.source: Planning Commission/NITI Aayog poverty committees; OPHI-UNDP Global MPI; NITI National MPI reports (verified Sep 2026)

items.question: Examine the nature of unemployment in India and critically assess the role of employment-guarantee and skilling programmes, in light of recent policy changes such as the PLFS revamp and the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025.
items.modelAnswer:
Unemployment in India is **structural and multi-layered** rather than merely cyclical. The dominant forms are **disguised unemployment** in agriculture (surplus workers with near-zero marginal productivity), **structural** unemployment from skill-job mismatch, **educated (white-collar)** unemployment among qualified youth, and growing **technological** displacement from automation. Underlying causes include **rapid labour-force growth**, an **education-skill gap**, sluggish non-farm job creation and a vast **informal sector**, producing the **jobless growth** paradox — high GDP growth without proportionate employment. The challenge is sharpest for **youth (15-29)** and reflected in a **low female labour-force participation rate**.

Accurate diagnosis needs good data. The **PLFS**, launched in 2017 to replace the NSSO's quinquennial surveys, is now far more responsive: from **January 2025** it releases **monthly** estimates for both rural and urban areas on a calendar-year basis, enabling near-real-time tracking of LFPR, WPR and the unemployment rate. This addresses a long-standing critique that policy flew blind between five-yearly surveys.

On interventions, **wage-employment** guarantees have been the backbone of rural livelihood security. **MGNREGA (2005)** provided a legal right to **100 days** of work, one-third reserved for women, and acted as a **demand-driven safety net** — proven during COVID-19. Reforms such as the mandatory **Aadhaar-Based Payment System (2024)** curbed leakages but raised exclusion concerns. In **2025**, Parliament repealed MGNREGA through the **Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act (VB-G RAM G)**, reframing the scheme as a broader **employment-and-livelihood mission** — a shift that must be judged on whether it **preserves the justiciable guarantee and wage-payment timeliness** that made MGNREGA effective. On the supply side, **skilling and self-employment** programmes — **Skill India/PMKVY, DDU-GKY, PMEGP, Stand-Up India** and the **e-Shram** database — target employability and entrepreneurship, though placement quality and scale remain weak.

A credible strategy must combine **labour-intensive manufacturing, quality skilling aligned with industry, formalisation of the informal sector, and higher female participation**. For **Andhra Pradesh**, with its strength in **aquaculture, horticulture and services**, aligning skilling missions with these sectors and the **Vizag-Chennai Industrial Corridor** offers the most direct route from disguised rural underemployment to productive non-farm jobs.
keyPoints: Indian unemployment is largely structural: disguised (agriculture), structural (skill mismatch), educated and technological.
Causes: labour-force growth, skill gap, weak non-farm jobs, informal-sector dominance — the jobless-growth paradox.
PLFS (2017) replaced quinquennial NSSO surveys; from Jan 2025 gives monthly rural+urban estimates for timely data.
MGNREGA (2005) gave a demand-driven legal right to 100 days' work; ABPS (2024) cut leakages but risked exclusion.
VB-G RAM G Act 2025 repealed MGNREGA, reframing it as a broader employment-livelihood mission — judge on guarantee retention.
Skilling/self-employment: Skill India/PMKVY, DDU-GKY, PMEGP, Stand-Up India, e-Shram — placement and scale remain weak.
AP angle: align skilling with aquaculture, horticulture, services and the Vizag-Chennai Industrial Corridor.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Unemployment in India; MoSPI PLFS revamp; Ministry of Rural Development / VB-G RAM G Act 2025 (verified Sep 2026)
